commons:96246736.summary: Christ hangs on a rough-hewn cross whose trunk still bears the stumps of lopped branches, his head bowed and his body drawn in fluttering, nervous line. The Virgin and John, each holding a book, stand on either side, two figures in roundels appear above the cross, and a small figure kneels clasping the foot of the cross. Painted for a devout patroness, the page invites the viewer into the same close, personal devotion to the crucified Lord.
facts: The manuscript belonged to Judith of Flanders, Countess of Northumbria and a noted patron, who commissioned and collected illuminated books; her Gospels are now in the Morgan Library & Museum.
The tree-like 'rough-hewn' cross is a motif studied in Jennifer O'Reilly's essay on the rough-hewn cross in Anglo-Saxon art, from which this image is reproduced.
commons:96246736.notes: Commons describes the page as a 'Descent from the Cross', but it is clearly a Crucifixion (Christ still on the cross). The kneeling figure at the foot is often identified as the patroness Judith, but this was not confirmed from a source read here. The Morgan's own record could not be accessed (bot check); date c. 1065 and Canterbury follow the Commons record.

walters:71.122.summary: Two scenes of the Passion are stacked on this small ivory leaf. Above, Joseph of Arimathea embraces the body of Christ as it is lowered from the cross, while the Virgin takes his hanging arm and another mourner stands at the left; below, Christ stands bound to a column between two tormentors who raise their scourges. The open compositions and large figures give the little panel a monumental quality.
facts: The Walters assigns the leaf to the 'Rose Group' of French Gothic ivories, named after the rosettes on their mouldings, as seen here.
The museum notes two unusual features: a single element of landscape beneath the feet of one tormentor, and roped sides not found on other examples of the group.
walters:71.122.notes: Museum date 1301–1325; the 8th-century date in our data was an import error. The hinges show it was one wing of a diptych.
